papers.title: A versatile set of computational tools for inference of genetic ancestry from human molecular data
papers.abstract: Molecular properties of human diseases and conditions often exhibit dependence on the genetic ancestry of the donor. In order to make more human molecular data available for ancestry-informed research, we developed a set of software tools termed Robust Ancestry Inference using Data Synthesis (RAIDS) for inference of genetic ancestry from sequence data that pose challenges to genotyping. Here we describe a recent expansion and refinement of RAIDS, applicable to nucleic-acid sequence data resultant from a broad range of experimental strategies. These strategies currently include whole-genome, whole-exome, and targeted gene panel sequencing, RNA-Seq, including single-cell RNA-Seq, chromatin-accessibility (ATAC-Seq), and protein-binding (ChIP-Seq) assays. RAIDS inferential tools perform robustly in the presence of somatic nucleic-acid alterations caused by cancer and under the conditions of extreme non-uniformity of sequence read coverage, yielding both global ancestry and ancestral admixtures of the donor. RAIDS is available as an eponymous Bioconductor package.

papers.title: Imputing relative abundances via Gaussian random fields
papers.abstract: Longitudinal studies with human participants frequently face the challenge of missing samples, which lead to incomplete trajectories of participant biomarkers and a reduction in data size. Existing approaches focus on single-variable imputation or model features one at a time, while neural networks typically require a large number of parameters and substantial training data. To address these challenges, we present an explainable model for multiple imputation of compositional samples based on a Gaussian random field (GRF). The model is specifically designed for longitudinal data: it incorporates participant-specific information and accounts for both temporal dependence across repeated observations and within-sample correlations, while using a moderate number of parameters. By coupling the GRF with sparse activation functions, the framework outputs sum-constrained compositions and explicitly models zero inflation. Under the Aitchison and Jensen--Shannon distances, our framework achieves imputation accuracy comparable to that of an observation-carrying baseline, while overcoming its static nature by modeling temporal trajectories and multivariate correlations. The resulting multiple imputations allow us to reconstruct complete datasets for downstream analysis and uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate the practical utility of our framework on gut microbiome datasets, restoring incomplete time series and achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.72 in predicting food allergy in infants (sensitivity 0.8) and of 0.64 in forecasting postpartum depression.

papers.title: BioMod: Biological Module Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Modeling
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.

papers.title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
papers.abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.

papers.title: Optimizing copy number profiles for tumor cell phylogeny inference from low-coverage single-cell sequencing data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Accurate reconstruction of tumor cell phylogenies is crucial for understanding cancer evolutionary dynamics, inferring intra-tumor heterogeneity, and designing effective and personalized cancer treatment strategies. One of the most promising and cost-effective approaches for reconstructing tumor phylogenies for large numbers of cells is to use copy number alteration (CNA) data obtained from low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing of sampled tumor cells. However, error and uncertainty in inferred copy number profiles (CNPs), resulting from low sequence coverage, can have a drastic negative effect on the reconstruction accuracy of tumor cell phylogenies. Results: In this work, we show that careful selection of bin size, a critical tuning parameter for inferring CNPs, is necessary to maximize the accuracy of tumor cell phylogeny inference. Specifically, we (i) use three previously published low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing datasets from real tumors to demonstrate that even small changes in bin size can have a drastic impact on downstream tumor phylogeny reconstruction, (ii) show that this effect persists even when using simulated low-coverage datasets generated under idealized conditions with minimal noise, and (iii) propose a simple computational approach to select bin sizes that maximize tumor phylogeny accuracy. Our experiments span a wide range of bin sizes and account for the impact of various factors including coverage-level, phylogeny reconstruction method, and CNP inference method, and explicitly account for phylogenetic reconstruction uncertainty. Our evaluation of the proposed computational approach for bin size selection shows that it can significantly improve tumor cell phylogeny reconstruction accuracy compared to baseline methods. Availability: Freely available from https://github.com/Tanveer14/BinSelector.

papers.title: Efficient approximate Bayesian inference for large, heterogeneous biological datasets
papers.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a route to connect biological data with mechanistic models. At the frontier of biology, datasets continue to grow in scale and richness, and increasingly record heterogeneity between individual observations that a mechanistic model can take into account. Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) remains a popular approach to SBI due to its ease of use, but incorporating this heterogeneity often requires a separate simulation of each observation, which is prohibitively expensive at scale. A previously proposed technique, minibatch Sequential Monte Carlo ABC (SMC ABC), reduces this cost by simulating a fixed-size random subset of observations for each proposal, at the price of sampling noise that limits precision. Here, we present an adaptive minibatch approach that uses small batches during early exploration and increases the batch size as the posterior is refined. The adaptive batch size is set by the target precision and does not grow with the size of the dataset, so the savings over full-data SMC ABC increase for larger datasets. We demonstrate the method on synthetic biological models and on real single-cell gene-expression data that vary in scale and type of heterogeneity, including cell geometry and initial condition. In each case, the adaptive scheme obtains posteriors close to those of full-data SMC ABC at a fraction of the cost. Altogether, adaptive minibatching improves the tradeoff between speed and precision in SMC ABC and opens the door to mechanistic inference on large, heterogeneous biological datasets.

papers.title: Surrogate variables and the risk of overfitting in neuropsychiatric gene expression analyses
papers.abstract: The reproducibility crisis in biomedical research calls for re-evaluation of how common analytic approaches affect results. One such approach, surrogate variable analysis (SVA), is widely used to adjust for unmeasured drivers of variation in transcriptomic differential expression analyses. We systematically quantified the impact of SVA using synthetic data with known ground truth and fourteen brain RNA-seq and microarray datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Parkinson's disease. In synthetic data, SVA usage frequently led to high false positive rates. This issue was not revealed by standard diagnostics nor resolved by strategies such as maximizing cross-dataset signal correlation. In real data, using SVA reduced cross-cohort reproducibility of differential expression signatures regardless of the number of surrogate variables included. These findings show that SVA risks inducing overfitting at realistic signal levels, advocating for a cautious, case-by-case application, with a preference for modeling known covariates.

papers.title: scGSCA: gene-set differential co-expression analysis for single-cell RNA sequencing data
papers.abstract: Understanding disease-associated pathway coordination requires distinguishing phenotype-related co-expression changes from differences across cellular contexts while accounting for cells sampled from the same subject. Bulk gene-set co-expression methods do not directly address the sparse counts, single-cell distributional noise, subject-level dependence, and cell-type heterogeneity of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. We developed single-cell gene-set co-expression analysis (scGSCA), a framework for pathway-level differential co-expression analysis in scRNA-seq data. scGSCA fits gene-wise zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models with subject-level random effects and computes gene-set co-expression statistics from quantile residual correlations. It provides an overall differential gene-set co-expression analysis and an interaction test to assess whether the co-expression pattern between two cell types varies by sample phenotype. We applied scGSCA to tumor-normal gastric, breast-subtype, and lung-skin comparisons with matched bulk and scRNA-seq data. The overall test identified signals not captured in bulk analysis, including Axon guidance in gastric cancer and estrogen-response, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and TNF/NF-{kappa}B pathways in breast cancer. The interaction test further identified co-expression contrasts across cell types. scGSCA extends gene-set co-expression analysis to single-cell data while retaining subject-level structure and cell-type-specific context. scGSCA is freely available as an open-source R package.

papers.title: CLARA: Compound Library Active Learning with Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Batch active learning for ligand discovery requires a recurring decision about whether to exploit high predicted affinity, reduce model uncertainty, or broaden chemical coverage. We test whether a language model can make this strategy-level decision while candidate ranking and label revelation remain controlled by a deterministic Gaussian-process environment. Across four protein targets, ten paired seeds, and a 360-compound assay budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent outperformed random sampling in all 40 matched campaigns. Its final top-2% recall was 0.412 on D2R, 0.374 on Mpro, 0.448 on TYK2, and 0.683 on USP7. It was statistically tied with the strongest fixed policy on Mpro and USP7 but underperformed target-specific leaders on D2R and TYK2. The agent shifted from exploration-oriented early batches toward exploitation and produced 686 testable threshold claims with an 86.3% atomic success rate, although 19.8% of forecasts were not numerically scorable. In 200 prespecified information-ablation campaigns, removing uncertainty, diversity, or memory caused only small endpoint changes, while shuffling explanatory evidence reproduced the full allocation path in 39 of 40 paired campaigns. A deterministic 80% availability constraint reduced recall on every target but preserved the target-dependent pattern of wins and losses. These results support language-model strategy control as a feasible and auditable layer.

papers.title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Novel Inhibitors Targeting the Thiamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Bacteria
papers.abstract: Current generation antibiotics are limited by poor target selectivity and are often mismanaged, leading to widespread antimicrobial resistance. The bacterial thiamine biosynthesis pathway offers compelling alternative since it is highly essential for bacterial survival and yet absent in humans. Genetic perturbations within pathway lead to documented auxotrophy and virulence defects, indicating low mutational tolerance within this pathway. Thiamine phosphate synthase is a key bottleneck enzyme performing the crucial role of coupling thiazole and pyrimidine moieties to form thiamine monophosphate. To develop a suitable inhibitor against it, a structure-based drug design pipeline was implemented. High-throughput virtual screening of nearly 1.5 million molecules provided sufficient exploration of chemical space. Further, R-group substitution was utilized for lead optimization. Structure-Activity Relationship analysis upon molecular mutants reveals patterns among R-group interactions to catalytic residues across various scaffolds. Additionally, ADMET screening and validation using molecular dynamics simulations resulted in a potent orally bioavailable broad-spectrum bactericidal molecule.

papers.title: High-performance xenograft read-sorting for DNA methylation analysis
papers.abstract: Xenograft sorting tools separate sequenced DNA reads by species. We have enhanced the computational method and tool Xengsort to enable efficient epigenetic profiling of patient-derived xenograft models; it now supports cytosine-converted whole genome or reduced-representation data. Benchmarking Xengsort against several established methods (ICRG, bamcmp, XenofilteR) revealed consistently high accuracy across tools, but Xengsort outperformed the other tools in computational efficiency due to its alignment-free design.

papers.title: Probing isn't Causality in Molecular Models
papers.abstract: Linear probes establish whether a chemical variable can be recovered from a molecular representation; they do not establish how that variable contributes to subsequent predictions. We replace a concept-associated scalar component at an intermediate block and measure the change through a separately fitted downstream outcome readout. Comparisons with random directions and architecture-matched random encoders distinguish recoverability, intervention selectivity, and a pretraining-associated selectivity advantage. In Uni-Mol, block-12 total-distortion edits predict the observed energy-change sign for 97.6% of held-out pairs, with Spearman $rho=0.787$. Structure-clustered intervals for the primary direction and encoder contrasts exclude zero. A stricter 20-direction sensitivity analysis does not survive correction across six cells. A post-review analysis finds substantial concept--outcome alignment; intervention effects persist after removal of the same-block outcome direction, but this does not establish that subsequent encoder computation is necessary. In MolCLR, pretraining improves dipole recovery by $0.080,R^2$, whereas concept-minus-random sign-accuracy contrasts are $0.029$ and $-0.015$ at the two tested blocks. Their paired uncertainty is unresolved, so they do not establish an absence of selective effects. We propose an operational evidence ladder whose conclusions are conditional on the concept, intervention, control family, and fitted readout.

papers.title: UPLiFT: Uncertainty Parameterized Activation for Lightweight Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Learned protein representations contribute to the broad utility of pretrained protein language models (PLMs), often enhanced by task-specific fine-tuning where parameter-efficient techniques are imperative due to large network size. Our work takes an orthogonal approach to such fine-tuning: rather than optimizing the network weights, we formulate adaptation as an optimization task over the parameterized activation space. Motivated by the prior work on curvature-tuning, we propose UPLiFT, Uncertainty Parameterized activation for Lightweight Fine-Tuning, with enhanced adaptation capacity when the underlying model--whether pretrained or randomly initialized--remains fixed, for significantly improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, its learnable non-linearity naturally allows to model uncertainty over the activation space through fine-tuning in a variational inference framework. Evaluation across multiple protein datasets shows that UPLiFT performs competitively while requiring 3-11x fewer trainable parameters than weight-only adaptations. Bayesian UPLiFT further improves calibration while largely preserving the predictive performance of deterministically fine-tuned models. The narrow predictive performance margin with the low-rank adaptation baseline in residue-level tasks highlights the potential of our proposed approach as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for PLM-based predictors.

papers.title: phyloDS: phylogeny-aware differential splicing across species, beyond reference annotations
papers.abstract: Alternative splicing diverges rapidly between species, yet its comparative analysis lags far behind that of gene expression: junction orthology is defined on a single reference genome, species are treated as independent samples, and detected shifts are rarely grounded in sequence-level evidence. We present phyloDS, an RNA-seq--driven framework that resolves all three limitations. phyloDS defines orthologous splice junctions on multiple sequence alignments of one-to-one orthologous genes, tests their differential usage with a regularized Ornstein--Uhlenbeck model, and cross-validates detected shifts against splice-site predictions made from genomic sequence alone. Applied to primate brain and rodent heart transcriptomes, phyloDS recovered up to 2.9-fold more shared orthologous splice junctions than a reference-based strategy and kept type~I error near nominal where competing methods inflate it more than two-fold. It identified 234 and 502 differentially used orthologous splice junctions in hominoids and mole-rats (86 and 141 unannotated), revealing a mitochondrial and contractile splicing signature in mole-rats.

papers.title: Application of Bayesian-Derived Gene Interaction Network and Subnetwork for Classification of Idiopathic Parkinson Disease with Biomarkers
papers.abstract: Given the expenses associated with Parkinson Disease (PD), it is imperative to develop a method for accurate diagnosis before emergence of motor symptoms. While there are tests that can measure early onset of PD, these tests still rely on subjective input from patients and can thus be biased. Factors influencing their accuracy include environmental agents such as education and culture. Thus, blood-based transcriptomic signatures are a promising direction for biomarkers in PD that are minimally invasive and more objective than clinical evaluation. In this paper, we analyzed gene expression from the PPMI cohort. Using a Bayesian framework, a gene interaction network was constructed to enhance differential expressed genes (DEG) analysis through signal diffusion. In tandem with clinical traits, 13 genes were selected for optimal discrimination using a random forest model. Within the holdout test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.972, outperforming contemporary models. The model performance demonstrates the potential of using blood-based transcriptomics to enhance clinical diagnosis of PD. Other genes recovered by network diffusion but missed by traditional DEG analysis are already validated as potential biomarkers in contemporary PD research. By combining transcriptomic signatures with clinical evaluation, accurate diagnosis of PD can happen before the major destruction of dopaminergic neurons, which is critical for effective intervention and treatment.

papers.title: AnnZarro: scalable, interactive exploration of cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships in single-cell data
papers.abstract: Cell-by-cell and gene-by-gene relationships, such as kernels and correlations, shape most single-cell analyses but are rarely inspected directly due to a lack of visualization tools that display them. AnnZarro is a point-and-click browser viewer that shows these matrices linked to an AnnData object's cells x genes data. Using AnnZarro, experimental biologists can explore data without code and computational biologists can probe the relationships behind their analyses. One focused cell and one focused gene drive every panel. Clicking a cell paints its row of any cell-by-cell matrix over an embedding or spatial coordinates; clicking a gene paints its row of any gene-by-gene matrix over a gene plot such as a volcano. The focus also links genes to the cells where they change, and cells to the genes that distinguish them. AnnZarro reads only the matrix rows and columns each panel displays from zarr stores and hence users can explore matrices far larger than memory on a laptop or a shared server. Large datasets open on a reproducible subset, and users step through the remaining cells in parts. On a laptop, a 100,000-cell part of Tahoe-100M opens in 4 s and stays interactive. With the subset switched off, AnnZarro draws all 95.6 million cells in one plot in about 5 to 7 s. This tutorial prepares a dataset with Kompot differential abundance and expression, a diffusion kernel and gene correlations, then explores it in six worked examples.

papers.title: Tensorizing Pairwise Structural Analysis: GPU-Accelerated RMSD and FCC Clustering in HADDOCK3 Without Structural Regression.
papers.abstract: Integrative macromolecular docking pipelines generate thousands of candidate structural decoys, relying on downstream pairwise ensemble analysis, including Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD) matrices and Fraction of Common Contacts (FCC) clustering, to identify biologically relevant binding poses. However, pairwise structural comparisons scale quadratically (O(N^2)), and canonical workflows in HADDOCK3 historically rely on disk-bound trajectory serialization and iterative CPU set operations, creating a quadratic computational and storage bottleneck for large ensembles. Here, we demonstrate that these operations can be reformulated as continuous linear algebra on GPU-resident tensors: structural superposition via batched Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and residue contact overlap via binary matrix multiplication (M = A A^T). Across empirical benchmarks spanning N = 200 to 10,000 models (evaluating up to 49,995,000 decoy pairs), our GPU implementation achieves a 6.41-fold compute speedup on Apple Silicon (MPS) and up to 12.2-fold end-to-end acceleration in an N = 5,000 ablation on NVIDIA CUDA by eliminating trajectory disk I/O. Crucially, the implementation achieves zero downstream structural regression relative to canonical baselines, preserving identical cluster assignments (Adjusted Rand Index ARI = 1.0000, zero differing assignments) with sub-microangstrom RMSD concordance (Delta_max <= 4.07 x 10^-7 Angstrom on single-precision MPS; machine-precision Delta_max <= 8.88 x 10^-16 Angstrom on double-precision CUDA). The accelerated code, test suites, and benchmarking workflows are openly accessible on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license.

papers.title: Representing biological concepts as directions in foundation model embeddings
papers.abstract: Biological foundation models encode rich information about protein structure, function, and cellular state in high-dimensional embeddings, but accessing specific biological properties typically relies on additional, task-specific prediction models. Here, we show that diverse biological properties can be mapped to interpretable, reusable directions in embedding space. In the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) approach, examples representing a concept are distinguished from a background set using a linear model, and the resulting weight vector defines the CAV for that concept. In protein embeddings, CAVs recover Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission annotations, localize Pfam domains, reveal novel structural relationships, and capture DNA-binding and protein-interaction interface specificity. In single-cell embeddings, CAVs isolate cancer-associated expression transitions, and gene variation along these axes substantially agrees with conventional differential-expression analysis despite being a distinct computational approach. Together, these results establish concept directions as a common representation, enabling diverse biological features to be compared, localized, and manipulated.

papers.title: Reformulating Protein Corona Prediction as Universal Protein-conditioned Learning
papers.abstract: When nanoparticles enter biological environments, their surfaces are rapidly coated by proteins, forming a protein corona that governs their biological identity and downstream responses. Existing computational methods treat each protein as an independent prediction task, preventing the learning of shared adsorption principles and limiting generalization beyond experimentally characterized proteins. Here we introduce NanoPCT, a universal protein-conditioned learning framework that jointly models nanoparticle physicochemical properties and protein sequence representations. Using frozen ESM-2 embeddings and a joint interaction transformer, NanoPCT learns transferable representations of nano-bio interaction patterns across hundreds of proteins and maintains robust performance as protein diversity increases. The learned protein representation further enables zero-shot prediction for previously unseen proteins and biologically distinct protein groups through classifier reconstruction in embedding space. Beyond prediction, NanoPCT supports large-scale in silico inverse design and reveals consistent adsorption preferences between observed and unseen protein populations, suggesting that it captures transferable interaction patterns rather than protein-specific memorization. NanoPCT provides a unified framework for protein corona prediction, zero-shot generalization, and rational nanomaterial design.

papers.title: BioMeBar Indian Gut Reference Atlas: A Harmonised Multi-Cohort Healthy Microbiome Baseline and the Indian Gut Health Index
papers.abstract: Population-scale gut microbiome reference databases exist for Western and East Asian cohorts, yet no harmonised healthy baseline has been available for India's 1.4 billion inhabitants, whose diets span extreme geographic and cultural gradients. Western-derived reference ranges risk systematic misclassification when applied to Indian subjects. We harmonised eight published Indian healthy-gut microbiome cohorts (1,672 samples from 1,456 unique individuals , 20 geographic locations, six zones) onto a common NCBI family-level taxonomy axis. Raw 16S rRNA amplicon data were reprocessed through a uniform QIIME 2 / DADA2 / SILVA 138.1 pipeline where raw sequences were available; author-provided taxonomic tables from MetaPhlAn, HITChip, and RDP-based pipelines were retained and mapped via a four-step resolution cascade (exact match, synonym lookup, genus-to-family fallback, Unassigned). We defined the Indian Gut Health Index (IGHI), a four-component composite score (diversity, taxon balance, core membership, community typicality) calibrated against geography-stratified healthy Indian norms. The unified matrix comprised 380 bacterial families, of which 17 constituted the pan-Indian core ([≥]80% prevalence; Lachnospiraceae 100%, Prevotellaceae 99.5%). PERMANOVA confirmed significant compositional differences across geographies (pseudo-F = 43.4, p = 0.001) and cohorts (pseudo-F = 89.6, p = 0.001). Variance partitioning revealed that geography and cohort effects were deeply confounded (shared variance 30.4%; pure geography 4.1%, pure cohort 4.7%, residual 60.9%). Restricted permutation PERMANOVA confirmed city-level geographic signal after cohort correction (p = 0.001), but zone-level signal did not survive (p = 0.896). Two community types were identified: a Prevotellaceae-dominant type (69%) and an Oscillospiraceae-dominant type (31%), contrasting with the Western three-enterotype model. A Random Forest zone classifier achieved 68.4% balanced accuracy (null 16.6%), with Northeast subjects most distinguishable (F1 = 0.92). IGHI zone means ranged from 67.6 to 72.9 (inter-zone range 5.3 points), confirming effective geographic normalisation. Weight sensitivity analysis showed IGHI rankings were robust to moderate perturbation (Spearman {rho} [≥] 0.88 for five of six alternative schemes). The BioMeBarTM Indian Gut Reference Atlas provides the first pan-Indian harmonised healthy microbiome baseline, and the IGHI offers a population-calibrated scoring framework for gut health assessment in Indian individuals. The atlas, scoring model, and analysis code are openly available at https://github.com/TusharParihar128/BioMeBar_Indian_Healthy_Cohorts_datasets.

papers.title: Horizontal transfers can reveal ghost birth events and complete species trees
papers.abstract: Extinct and unsampled species vastly outnumber the species typically included in phylogenetic studies. Most of these so-called ``ghost lineages'' are unknown and, among them, those that are extinct may have left no trace in the fossil record. Horizontal gene transfers (HGTs), however, provide a potential source of information about these missing lineages, because transfers can connect sampled ancestral species to lineages outside the sampled species tree. Such transfers may leave observable signatures in gene trees. Here, we formalize this signal under idealized models of duplication, transfer, and loss, and characterize the information that can be retrieved about the complete species tree (containing ghost and non-ghost lineages) thanks to sampled gene trees and sampled species trees (containing only the non-ghost lineages). We establish four identifiability results, assuming an infinite number of gene families and errorless dated gene trees. First, transfers identify the lineage through time (LTT) curve of the complete tree, averaged over each time interval induced by the nodes of the sampled species tree. Second, in the presence of transfers, the distribution of node heights in sampled gene trees uniquely determines the internal speciation times of the complete species tree, including ghost speciations. Third, these hidden speciation times suffice to restore identifiability of birth-death-sampling parameters, through a reduction to a recent theorem of Dieselhorst and Stadler. Finally, when duplication, transfer, and loss rates are known constants and the transfer rate is non-zero, the distribution of sampled gene trees almost surely uniquely determines the topology and branch lengths of the complete species tree, including all ghost branches. These results provide a theoretical basis for using signatures left by HGTs in gene trees to recover information about extinct and unsampled lineages, and suggest ways in which this signal could be exploited in practice.

papers.title: Predicting cyanobacterial oxic diazotrophy and prioritizing candidate protein families beyond known Nif proteins
papers.abstract: Diazotrophic cyanobacteria must reconcile oxygenic photosynthesis with the oxygen sensitivity of nitrogenase. Engineering studies have demonstrated nitrogenase activity in a non-diazotrophic cyanobacterium while highlighting the importance of accessory functions and oxygen management. Robust aerobic nitrogen fixation remains challenging, motivating systematic identification of candidate support functions beyond the canonical Nif machinery. We modeled nifHDK-defined diazotrophic potential from protein-family presence or absence in 426 cyanobacterial assemblies. Four classifiers evaluated with genus-blocked cross-validation achieved mean ROC AUCs of 0.853 to 0.893, with purity and genus-breadth filters fitted within training folds. Restricting the panel to 401 assemblies with current NCBI status gave AUCs of 0.806 to 0.881. Family-content logistic regression outperformed a genome-size-only baseline across ten genus partitions. Two inventories describe candidates across the full panel: 981 high-purity families and 473 families with positive residual associations (accompanied by three ubiquitous controls). Model importance orders the residual-association inventory. A separate heuristic score combines inventory membership with proteomics, condensate-driver ranks and genus-based morphotype proxies to prioritize 167 families for experiments. Proteomics annotations tracked detection opportunity; the condensate contrast between inventories attenuated after prevalence adjustment. These annotations help choose experiments but do not independently validate accessory functions. Protein-family content predicts nifHDK-defined diazotrophic potential, with performance sensitive to assembly inclusion, taxonomy, genome size and taxonomic weighting. The two candidate inventories distinguish high carrier purity from residual association, providing complementary resources for prioritizing previously uncharacterized functions associated with cyanobacterial oxic diazotrophy.

papers.title: Activation of Disease-Associated Polycystin-1 Mutants by Binding of Stalk-derived Agonist Peptides
papers.abstract: Polycystin-1 (PC1) functions as an atypical G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) with an autocatalytic GAIN domain that cleaves PC1 into extracellular N-terminal (NTF) and membrane-embedded C-terminal (CTF) fragments. Mutations in PC1 are responsible for 85% of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) cases. Activation of signaling by PC1 CTF has been shown to be allosterically mediated by a stalk tethered agonist (TA) and to be prevented by mutations of the stalk. Soluble, synthetic peptides derived from the PC1 stalk were also shown to re-activate signaling by a stalkless CTF mutant. Here, we have investigated the ability of selected stalk peptide agonists p9, p15 or p17 to re-activate signaling by PC1 CTF with ADPKD-associated missense mutations, G3052R or R3063C. Biochemical experimental data showed that each of the three stalk peptides was able to significantly reactivate signaling by the CTF-R3063C mutant. In contrast, signaling by CTF-G3052R could only be rescued by treatment with p17. In parallel, we employed peptide docking and novel Peptide Gaussian-accelerated Molecular Dynamics (Pep-GaMD) simulations to elucidate the binding conformations of p9, p15 and p17 to the PC1 mutants. The simulation findings were highly consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, Pep-GaMD revealed binding conformations of the agonist peptides and important low-energy conformational states of the PC1 CTF, as well as their critical residue interactions. Overall, our complementary approach provides important mechanistic insights into the re-activation of PC1 disease-associated mutants by stalk-derived peptide agonists. Such insights are expected to be valuable for the future design and development of peptide modulators targeting PC1 for an effective ADPKD therapeutic treatment.

papers.title: Benchmarking single-cell foundation models reveals an advantage in the low-data regime for cell-type and disease-state prediction
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models perform well on cell-type classification, but their value for disease-state prediction and their advantage over classical representations remains unclear. We benchmarked cell-representations from four foundation models using logistic regression, on 868 disease-prediction tasks (82 datasets) and 65 cell-type datasets from CELLxGENE. With full data, the baseline (log-normalized counts) outperformed the best model (TranscriptFormer-Sapiens) for cell type and matched it for disease. However, with few labeled cells, TranscriptFormer-Sapiens significantly outperformed the baseline in both tasks up to ~102 samples per class. Our comprehensive zero-shot benchmark identifies the data-scarce regime as a domain where Single-cell foundation models truly show advantage.

papers.title: Probabilistic Modelling of Base Editing Efficiency and Bystander Outcome Composition
papers.abstract: Abstract. Base editors install single nucleotide substitutions without a double strand break or donor template, but editing at multiple susceptible positions can generate bystander alleles. Predicting the frequency of an intended outcome therefore requires both editing efficiency and the composition of edited products. Here we present crispAIBE, a probabilistic framework that uses separately trained transformer convolutional networks to predict Dirichlet distributions for editing efficiency and conditional allele composition. Split-conformal density-level regions are calibrated on data reserved from model selection, with composition thresholds fitted by outcome-set size. On held-out data, crispAIBE achieves Pearson correlations of 0.669 for efficiency and 0.896 for composition on measured allele sets, with empirical coverages of 0.902 and 0.906 at a nominal level of 0.90. On the published CRISPRon-BE benchmark, with test protospacers excluded from training, crispAIBE ranks first in seven of eight comparisons under the two-column Pearson statistic and first or second in seven of eight under the rank statistic. Within predicted-efficiency quintiles, the largest- and smallest-region deciles differ 1.9-fold in mean absolute error on average, compared with 1.7-fold for a boundary-distance ranking. When evaluated on U2OS, which was excluded from training, larger predictive regions were associated with larger absolute prediction errors. Local calibration with 100 U2OS protospacers yields median empirical coverage of 0.918 at the nominal 0.90 level. The crispAIBE repository is https://github.com/furkanozdenn/crispAIBE.

papers.title: Beyond Ramachandran distributions: quantifying secondary structure effects on amino acids and their pairs in the full torsional space
papers.abstract: The Ramachandran diagram has long served for understanding protein secondary structure elements (SSEs), despite the multitude of factors contributing to their occurrence. Starting from recentlyintroduced circula-based multivariate torsion-angle distribution (CBMD) mixture models -- accommodating covariance structure in the full torsion-angle space of amino acids, we define continuous densities for the 20 amino acids and 400 amino-acid pairs in dimension up to 14, conditioned by SSE labels. Projecting these higher-dimensional distributions onto the classical Ramachandran diagram reveals how secondary structures in the protein universe emerge from amino-acid-dependent conformational preferences reflecting influences beyond backbone dihedrals alone. Our analysis links the traditional geometric description of local protein structure to modern statistical models of the full conformational space of amino acids and amino-acidpairs, while providing a framework for generating protein conformations consistent with any given secondary structure environment -- a feature that remains difficult to enforce explicitly in current AI-based generative models.

papers.title: STARgrid: an open-source pipeline from Visium HD sequencing reads to count matrices
papers.abstract: In Visium HD, transcript positions are computed from sequenced barcodes, which are matched to a list of coordinate barcodes that map to a grid of capture locations. Quantifying reads and assigning their positions have relied on Space Ranger, whose end-user licence prohibits modification and whose published source cannot be redistributed. We present STARgrid, the first open-source pipeline that takes Visium HD FASTQ files from Flex or RNA-seq based quantitation to count matrices at 2, 8 and 16 um; it is part of STAR Suite. On three human slides its output agrees closely with Space Ranger's (correlations of gene totals are at least 0.9989), and STARgrid takes 20-35% less wall time under the tested configurations. STARgrid assigns each read barcode to the coordinate barcode with the most similar sequence, as assessed by edit distance. In an examination of Space Ranger's per-read output on one further slide, Space Ranger does the same for most reads, with two differences. First, where two coordinate barcodes overlap, the shorter being the longer without its first base, Space Ranger records the shorter barcode, although the longer one matches with fewer edits; in all, Space Ranger's location is not among the closest for 0.5980% of the reads that our decoder can place. Second, Space Ranger settles each read on its own, recording one location or none, and leaves 0.2916% of these reads without a location; STARgrid keeps every matching location and chooses among them for each molecule, using all its reads. Our molecule totals are 1.9-7.6% above Space Ranger's. The larger source of this difference is probably that we resolve location for each molecule and not for each read; STAR Suite's own gene assignment and molecule counting may also contribute. The counts that STARgrid adds behave like signal. On H&E images of the same sections they fall in cells at nearly the rate of the counts that both pipelines report. Against an adjacent Xenium section of one slide, our counts are closer to Xenium than Space Ranger's for 15 of the 20 genes of a cancer gene panel that Xenium measures most abundantly (P = 0.0414). The added counts therefore appear to improve the measurement of cancer-associated expression. These results are preliminary, but the method is now open, and every comparison reported here can be repeated, extended and improved upon.

papers.title: genomeRxiv: a genome-based identification web server that bridges the gap between taxonomy and strain typing
papers.abstract: Precise identification depends on highly resolved classification. Therefore, whole genome-based strain typing schemes have been implemented for identification of the most important microbial human pathogens. However, there are no dedicated typing schemes for the majority of prokaryotic human, animal, and plant pathogens, or for non-pathogenic microbes, often limiting their identification to taxonomic classification tools that have the species as the smallest unit. To address this deficiency, we created the genomeRxiv web server which contains over 350,000 genomes and leverages the average nucleotide identity (ANI)-based Life Identification Number (LIN) approach, allowing users to identify prokaryotic genomes in real time from approximately genus-rank to near strain-level resolution. LINs are overlaid with circumscriptions of species and infraspecies classes, integrating taxonomy with strain typing. Metadata and distance trees are visualized to complement inferred phylogenetic relationships with epidemiological and ecological information. A command line tool is provided for users to upload k-mer sketches of unpublished genomes and associated metadata, facilitating epidemiological investigations without the need to share complete DNA sequences. In conclusion, genomeRxiv constitutes a much-needed resource for precise, rapid identification of the many prokaryotes not included in any pathogen-specific typing scheme.

papers.title: tRNAZAP: Deep learning toolkit for nanopore tRNA signal analysis
papers.abstract: tRNA are short, ~76 nucleotide-long, modification-rich molecules that play an important role in protein translation. Nanopore sequencing is the only platform capable of directly sequencing full-length, native tRNA molecules. This capability is enabled by splinted ligation of tRNA-specific adapters. As a result, the measured ionic current signal reflects a composition of both adapter and tRNA sequence features. Despite these advantages, analysis of nanopore tRNA sequencing data poses distinct computational challenges. Existing ionic current-based signal-to-sequence decoding (basecalling) models are optimized for mRNA and perform suboptimally on short, modification-dense RNA such as tRNA. Furthermore, alignment algorithms for reference-guided analysis of short-length reads are not optimized for nanopore reads with lower accuracy than Next-generation sequencing reads. To overcome these limitations, domain-specific computational approaches are required. We present tRNAZAP, a nanopore ionic current signal analysis toolkit designed to enable precise reference-guided sequence alignment. tRNAZAP operates directly on raw ionic current signals and decomposes the analysis into two complementary tasks: 1) segmentation of adapter and tRNA regions, and 2) tRNA classification, both implemented using transformer-based models. The segmentation component isolates the tRNA signal portion and extracts the corresponding nucleotide sequence as the alignment query, while the classification component identifies the tRNA type as the alignment reference without requiring sequence-level information. Together, these outputs allow direct optimal pairwise alignment between the tRNA subsequence of the full query and reference sequences. Trained on in vitro transcribed RNA data and evaluated on yeast tRNA, these models achieved ~98% classification accuracy and intersection-over-union of ~0.98 for segmentation.

papers.title: Probing Physical Intuition in Large Language Models through Partner-Dependent Mutation Prediction
papers.abstract: Structure-guided mutation design requires relating a proposed substitution to its molecular environment to anticipate its effects. Existing evaluations of large language models (LLMs) in protein engineering emphasize sequence-based prediction or tool-integrated workflows, leaving unclear whether LLMs themselves can infer mutation effects from structural evidence without dedicated predictors. We evaluate physical intuition-qualitative reasoning that connects structural observations with molecular interaction principles-using a benchmark that tests the same substitution in the same protein across different binding partners, with predictions based on local atomic coordinates and no dedicated mutation-effect predictors. In the tested comparisons, the best-performing LLM achieved group accuracy comparable to the evaluated energy predictors and Biomni, an LLM-driven tool workflow, while the methods differed in their prediction patterns. Most evaluated LLMs achieved higher group accuracy for larger affinity improvements. Structural interventions support selective dependence on mutation-site and partner information, while assessable structural claims largely agree with the supplied coordinates. These findings support direct LLM structural reasoning as a basis for developing rational mutation-design tools that connect molecular observations with partner-specific effects.
